title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

reading.body:
This is an impersonation failure built on synthetic media. A generated video presented a well-known financial sector figure as endorsing an investment, and the fabricated endorsement was the entry point of the fraud rather than a detail inside it. The victim's decision to invest followed from believing a person they recognised had put their name to the offer.

The impersonation did its work at the top of the funnel, in an advert. Everything after that ran through ordinary fraud channels, WhatsApp contact, multiple online accounts opened at the fraudsters' direction, remote access to the victim's computer given under the pretence of help with the investment, and borrowed money sent to accounts controlled by criminals. Catching it required verifying two things independently, that the person in the video had actually endorsed the investment and that the provider was authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority. The police account places both checks after the loss, which is where they are normally placed when the advert itself carries no verified link to the person depicted.

What is not established is any involvement by the figure whose likeness was used. The Police Service of Northern Ireland did not name them, and the reporting of other scams using named financial experts concerns different cases. The account is a police description of a fraud, not a finding against any person or platform.

reports.title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

summary:
A person in the Ards and north Down area lost £250,000 after an AI generated video scam. The Police Service of Northern Ireland said the victim saw an advert that appeared to feature a well-known financial sector personality and promoted an investment with large returns. After a small initial investment, fraudsters contacted the victim on WhatsApp and urged more payments. They persuaded the victim to open multiple online accounts and gave them remote access to a computer, saying they were helping with the investment.

Police called it a sophisticated and substantial fraud. The victim was encouraged to borrow money, and funds went to accounts controlled by criminals. The PSNI did not name the celebrity, though BBC News NI has seen scams using financial experts such as Martin Lewis, Peter Jones and Steven Bartlett. Police advised people to independently verify who they are dealing with and check that financial services providers are authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority. A superintendent also urged people to stop and check financial activity and for families to talk about fraud.
